en: Preface to the Record of What Was Personally Heard Regarding the *Treatise on Birth in the Pure Land as Non-Birth*.
As for the phrase "personally heard," this indicates that the transmission was received without error. Regarding the teaching:

at the age of seven, he left the household life and followed his preceptor, the Great Monk, to Puci Temple in Kuacang to hear lectures on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*. At the conclusion of those lectures, he heard this treatise, which he studied with uninterrupted diligence.
For ten days, his literary exposition was most eloquent and his elucidation of the meaning was most refined.
Among the assembly listening beneath him, there was not a single person whose body or mind felt weary, nor anyone who did not attain awakening.

Only Huijiao, whose spiritual faculties were dull and who, moreover, was a mere child lacking understanding—like a deaf-mute watching a performance, doing nothing more than following others in weeping or laughing—returned to Youxi.

As my years have gradually advanced, my desire for the Dharma has increased day by day. Not only have I listened and received it many times, but I have also repeatedly requested and inquired about it;
as I heard each point, I recorded it, until scattered leaves filled my boxes. There was no doubt that I did not resolve, nor any meaning that I did not examine in detail.
If these were not woven together and compiled, how could they benefit others or myself? As for the skillful use of local dialects...
I am clumsy. One might say that the responsibility lies with my own person; yet, as for my realization, it is subtle and faint. How could I dare present this to those of future wisdom?
Those who have entered the gate, please ascend directly to the hall and partake of the nectar of immortality. Various questions regarding the bridge are not what is urgent here.
Preface to the *Treatise on Birth in the Pure Land as Non-Birth*, composed by the junior disciple of Youxi at Mount Tiantai,
the śramaṇa Shoujiao, in the first month of spring in the sixth year of the Ming Tianqi era, the year of Bingyin.
Formerly, Yang Cigong said: "The writings that praise and assist the teachings and contemplations of Amitābha are as numerous as mountains;
yet, only the *Ten Doubts* (Shiyi lun) by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai stands preeminent. Who could have known that more than six hundred years after Yang Cigong..."

Furthermore, he brought forth the discourse on "Birth as Non-Birth" by our late Master Youxi. Encompassing the oceanic treasury of the Dharma with ten gates, he harmonized billions of lands within a single thought-moment.
He expanded upon what the ancients had not fully prepared and elucidated what people of today have never heard.
The profound meaning of rebirth is as clear as pointing at one's own palm; for it flows forth from his samādhi, and thus it is beyond the reach of conceptual thought. Birth.
In this present age, though they behold this treatise, none know to reflect deeply and seek birth [in the Pure Land]; is this not truly and most lamentable?
The reason for its inception truly began with my own lack of wisdom; therefore, I have hastened to commission the carving [of the woodblocks] to spread great compassion.

May all who wear hair and possess teeth, throughout the bounds of the future, universally partake of the milk of the Dharma and fully awaken to non-arising. As for praising these merits, it is as follows:

There are Buddhas throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each possessing a broad and long tongue. This hair-pathed ordinary person has merely sketched out its general outline.

Recorded by the disciple Wénlóng of Sìmíng, prostrating in homage, as a personal record of what was heard concerning the *Jìngtǔ shēng wúshēng lùn* (Treatise on Birth and Non-birth in the Pure Land), Volume One.
Recorded by the Dharma-grandson Youxi, who received the instruction.
△ Explanation of this treatise is divided into three sections. First, explaining the title of the treatise:
*The Treatise on Birth and Non-Birth in the Pure Land*.
The title consists of six characters, which encompass three layers of subject and object: namely, the producer and the produced, the fuser and the fused, and the expositor and the exposed.
First, regarding the producer and the produced: the two characters "Pure Land" (Jingtu) constitute the produced.
The single character "birth" (sheng) functions as that which gives birth; the Pure Land that is born from it is located to the west, passing through a hundred trillion Buddha-lands.
There is a world there named Sukhāvatī. In terms of its fundamental substance, this land possesses four types:

namely, the Land of Common Residence for Ordinary Beings and Sages, the Land of Residual Existence through Expedient Means, the Land of Adorned Retribution of Reality, and the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
Regarding those capable of generating [the aspiration for rebirth], namely the sentient beings of the Sahā world who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, their bodies are of two types:

first, the body of fragmented birth (*paricchinna-kāya*); second, the body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*). If one is a person subject to fragmented birth and death (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*), then all four kinds of pure lands may be sought as places of rebirth.
If one is a person subject to transformation birth and death (*pariṇāma-janma-maraṇa*), then one seeks rebirth only in the upper three lands. Or...
Regarding the two lands as one land: for example, Vaidehī was originally an ordinary person who, weary of the defilement of the shared realm, longed for the purity of the shared realm.
Merely by following the sixteen sublime contemplations she heard, the three delusions were suddenly shattered within a single mind; thus, right upon her seat—

Having realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one not only partially perceives the *sahōkai* (real recompense land) but also partially realizes the *jakukō* (land of serene light).

How could one who possesses a body of segmented birth (*bun-dan-shin*) seek rebirth in the four lands? Therefore, if one categorizes sentient capacities based on the segmented realm, the scope is broad;

if categorized based on the transformative realm (*en’eki*), the scope is narrow. Thus, within our Sahā world, the capacities for all four lands are complete; it simply depends upon whether one advances in understanding or applies oneself to practice.
Furthermore, these two types possess the capacities for all four teachings, as do the ordinary people who progress gradually;

although they possess the capacities for the four teachings and so forth, they all turn from the Small toward the Great and turn from the partial toward the Perfect, collectively constituting a single type of capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Second, regarding that which can integrate and that which is integrated: the three characters "Pure Land" and "birth" (*jìngtǔ shēng*) are that which is integrated;
the two characters "non-arising" (*wúshēng*) are that which integrates. This means using non-arising to integrate birth, and using birth to assist non-arising.

As it is said, "Principle is assisted by phenomena," such that although the One Way does not obstruct a thousand differences, phenomena attain integration through principle, so that even though there are ten thousand distinctions, they do not obstruct one another.
It is the state of being free from a single nature. This is indeed the principle of the True Suchness of non-arising.

If there were not the four kinds of pure lands and the two kinds of sentient beings capable of being born therein, then the principle of the inherent nature would remain forever obscured and unmanifest.
Nevertheless, although one knows that such things exist, if one does not know that phenomena are entirely identical to the principle, then as for the four kinds of pure lands and...
Now, these two types of capacities for birth remain ultimately separate and do not merge.
Therefore, a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who cultivates the Pure Land must use phenomena to assist principle, fervently seeking birth;
and use principle to merge with phenomena, such that birth is itself non-birth. Thus, although one is born throughout the day, one never departs from non-birth. Throughout the day...

Non-arising does not preclude arising. How could this be like those who prioritize principle, who at the mere mention of words treat non-being as their guest and insist that there is no land from which anything can arise;
or like those who prioritize phenomena, who at the mere mention of words take being as their master and insist that there is a land from which things can arise?
How could these be compared? Regarding the "Treatise on the Three Capacities" (*San-neng-lun*), that which is discussed consists of the five characters:

"Pure Land," "Birth," and "Non-birth. The word "treatise" (*lun*) itself is the means of discussion. This treatise takes the analysis of subtleties as its primary principle and the severing of delusions as its goal.
Through the analysis of subtleties, there is no principle that is not clarified; through the severing of delusions, there is no doubt that is not resolved. It may truly be called perfect.
This is the guide to the definitive meaning of sudden enlightenment and the core teaching on the Three Bodies and Four Lands. If one discusses the breadth and narrowness of these six characters:
the three characters "born in the Pure Land" are narrow from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), while the two characters "non-arising" are broad from the perspective of principle (*li*).

Furthermore, the three characters "born in the Pure Land" are broad because their phenomenal manifestations are manifold, whereas the two characters "non-arising" are [narrow] because the principle is one.

[If viewed] thus, it is narrow. Now, when phenomena are brought to fulfillment through principle, that principle is the principle within phenomena; when phenomena are harmonized through principle, those phenomena are the phenomena within principle.
When these are integrated and returned to their source, they are neither phenomenon nor principle, and neither broad nor narrow.
Furthermore, as for the five characters "Pure Land" and "birth in non-birth," they are broad insofar as they pertain to the principle and phenomena that are explained [by them].

Regarding the single character "treatise" (*lun*): if it refers only to the expressive words, it is narrow; yet if the treatise as the expressive vehicle encompasses the meanings and principles it expresses, it is broad.
The aforementioned five characters refer exclusively to that which is expressed, and thus what they contain is narrow.
If one says that there is no liberation apart from words, and takes those very words to be the *dhāraṇī*, then they are neither merely the expressive nor [merely the expressed].
That which is explained is neither broad nor narrow. If one were to subsume the ten gates under the subject matter of the treatise, each would have its own specific inclusion:
the Gate of the One True Dharma-realm (Eka-dharmadhātu) crowns the entire treatise and encompasses all five characters—“Pure Land,” “Birth,” and “Non-birth.
If it is the Gate of the Phenomenal Origination of Body and Land, then it pertains to the matter of the two characters “Pure Land” and the three aspects of mind and land.
This is the "Gate of Non-duality between Birth and the Buddha. It also encompasses both birth in the Pure Land and non-birth.
Fifth is "taking the Dharma-realm as the object of mindfulness. Sixth is "the mutual swallowing of the object and the contemplation. Seventh is "the naturalness of the three contemplations.

These three gates—namely, the three characters "birth," "non-birth," and [the third]—are each subsumed under two meanings. This is because the object of mindfulness and the contemplation of the object, as well as the three contemplations themselves, all pertain to the side of "birth."

As for the matter: if the Dharma-realm and its phenomena are such that they are mutually inclusive by their very nature (*dharmatā*), then the two characters "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) are merely peripheral matters.
The eighth [gate] is the spontaneous functioning of resonance; the ninth is the eternal oneness of this and that; and the tenth is the mutual presence of the present and the future.
These three gates are also subsumed under two categories. For instance, the six characters "resonance," "this and that," and "present and future" correspond respectively to "arising" and "purity."

The three characters for "Earth" (Dharmadhātu) pertain to the aspect of phenomena (*dharmāḥ*). If they are spontaneously, eternally one, and mutually inclusive, then this pertains to the two characters for "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*).
Were it otherwise, the title and the treatise would not correspond to one another;

how then could they harmonize the wondrous interpenetration of the general and the specific across both the summarized and the detailed sections? As for the fivefold explanation of the title, this is the method of Tiantai for interpreting the scriptures.

To apply general rules as an interpretation for this treatise ultimately results in forced and strained explanations; moreover, since the various masters have their own private expositions, they shall not be cited here at length.
The *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* states that there are five general purposes for composing a treatise: first, it is like gold being fashioned into vessels.
First, it is like a flower in full bloom, for it causes one to gain faith and understanding. Second, it is like the blossoming of a flower, for it reveals the truth to others.
Third, it is like a sumptuous meal, for one obtains the flavor of the Dharma. Fourth, it is like deciphering written characters, for it enables one to practice.

Fifth, it is like opening a jewel casket, for one attains actual realization. Now, this work likewise contains these five meanings; having gathered from various sutras, it has been composed as a single whole.
The Treatise is like gold fashioned into vessels. The treatise establishes ten sections (*mukha*); these sections elucidate manifold wonders, like flowers in full bloom.
The principle clarifies that nature is inherently complete; objects are realized as being but mind, like partaking of a delicious meal.

Having awakened to perfect cultivation, one knows that lands arise from the transformation of the mind, like deciphering written characters. Ultimate bliss within the nature is manifested through cultivation, like opening a treasure chest.
[This is] a casket. △ Second, the explanation of the author:
Written by the Tiantai Mountain monk Chuandeng of Youxi.
The Great Master’s courtesy name was Wujin; his alternative style name was Youmen. A native of Gumie in Sangu, he left the household life at Tiantai and resided there.
The wise master resided at Youxi Daochang for over forty years, propagating and disseminating the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school.

Among his writings are the *Lengyan jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra), the *Yuantong shu* (Commentary on the "Perfect Penetration" Chapter) and its preface, and the *Haiyin sanmei* (Ocean-Seal Samādhi);

these are known as the "Four Books on the Śūraṃgama. He also authored the *Jingming wuwo shu* (Commentary on the "Non-Self" Chapter of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) and the *Mituo yuanzhong chao* (Excerpts on the Perfect Center of Amitābha). [He also wrote the] *Yongjia*...

His collected commentaries include the *Prajñā-rongxin-lun* (Treatise on the Integration of Mind through Prajñā), the *Xing-shane-lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Good and Evil), and the *Youxi-wenji* (Collected Works of Youxi).

The present *Wusheng-lun* (Treatise on Non-arising) is one of these. The details of his lifelong practice and conduct are fully recorded in the "Stele of Gao-ming Temple" composed by the Grand Historian Han Quzhong, as well as in the *Jiaosi-ji* (Private Record of the Teaching) and his chronological biography; they are not recounted here in full.
△ Third, the explanation of the main text. When the Great Master lectured on this treatise, he had already established its divisions; now, following his original outline, nothing has been added.
The major sections are two: first, the homage and statement of intent; second, the establishment of the treatise according to its meaning. Within the first section, there are three parts.
First, prostrating to the Triple Gem. Within this, there are three parts. First, the Buddha-Gem of the two lands.
I prostrate to the Perfect Wisdom of the Able One (Śākyamuni), the Teacher of Infinite Life and Great Guide.
Regarding the practice of first taking refuge in the Triple Gem before composing a treatise or propagating a sutra, there are two intentions:

first, to establish the source of one's lineage so that it is known not to be a mere fabrication; second, to earnestly entreat the hidden protection [of the Buddhas] so as to avoid errors. My ancestors did likewise.
"Prostrating oneself" (*kai shou*) carries the meaning of "taking refuge" (*gui ming*). For a person, there is nothing more important than life;

for that life, there is nothing more honored than the head. Now, by bowing one’s most honored head at the feet of the Triple Gem, one expresses that one’s body and life have no other place of refuge, but are devoted solely to the Supreme Honored Ones of the Triple Gem—namely, Śākyamuni and the others.
This is the Teacher of this land. In the Sanskrit language he is called Śākyamuni, which here [in Chinese] means "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren) and "Silent and Still" (Jimo).

"Able Benevolent" manifests his function (*yòng*); "Silent and Still" reveals his essence (*tǐ*). Now, he is briefly referred to as "Able Benevolent" because while the wisdom of silence resides in stillness, the wisdom currently present resides in speaking;
therefore, he is called "Able Benevolent. "Able Benevolent" is a specific title (*bié-hào*), whereas his general title (*tōng-hào*) is...
There are ten [levels], the tenth of which is named Buddha. "Buddha" means awakening; it is also wisdom (*jñāna*). Tiantai’s commentary on this identifies six kinds of "suchness" (*tathatā*);
what is here termed "perfect wisdom" is ultimate awakening. Nevertheless, it is non-dual and undifferentiated from the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) of the capacities of sentient beings.
Therefore, the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies that the "Buddha of suchness" is the perfect wisdom that perfectly awakens to all phenomena.
It pervades all places without anything being unclear. The Great Master Fazhi said:

"This 'it' refers to such passages in the Great Sūtra as 'sentient beings are themselves Buddha,' which all denote that the original nature is perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), rather than the subtle fusion and identity of the three types of *prajñā*."
Wisdom is not yet called "perfect" (yuan) when it merely knows all phenomena.

When each and every phenomenon contains and receives all phenomena within itself—when the entire dharma is wisdom and the entirety of wisdom is dharma—and when all dualistic oppositions are severed, this is called "Perfect Enlightenment of All Phenomena" (yuanjue zhufa).

Thus, although sentient beings possess [this nature], they lack the power of the "cause of realization" (liaoyin). Consequently, they take the three types of wisdom entirely as the three delusions. Only Buddha after Buddha...
He is thus able to exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; his wisdom of the ultimate limit is perfected, and the fruit of various awakenings is fulfilled.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the One of Perfect Wisdom and the One of Immeasurable Life-Awakening—namely, Amitābha Buddha, the Teacher of the Western Land.

Since "Awakening" (*jue*) has already been used as a translation here, "Wisdom" (*zhi*) is employed above [in the title] as its substitute. Regarding the "Great Guide," the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) provides a detailed enumeration.
There are four kinds: namely, universal compassion, the forming of karmic connections, and the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real.

If categorized from the distant to the intimate, the present [teaching] concerns these two wisdoms, which also encompass the aforementioned two types of compassion. Amoghasiddhi (the Benevolent One) employs the provisional path to guide beings from this shore of the Sahā world;
Amitāyus (Immeasurable Life), however, employs the real path to lead them across to the other shore of Sukhāvatī.
Furthermore, Amitābha demonstrates the provisional through the real, while Amitāyus demonstrates the real through the provisional.
Thus, both World-Honored Ones may be called Great Guides of Perfect Wisdom; they exist in mutual relation yet do not occupy the same locus.
△ Next, the Dharma-treasures of the two lands.

The *An-yang* (Sukhāvatī) Mahāyāna Sūtra which has been expounded is the definitive meaning of the definitive meaning—the ultimate, sudden, and perfect means by which the Buddha delivers sentient beings.
He manifests benefit through both form and sound: "form" refers to manifesting his body and manifesting supernatural powers;
"sound" refers to speaking and remaining silent. The above was taking refuge in the Buddha, which is benefit through form; now we take refuge in the Dharma, which is [benefit] through sound.
"It is a benefit. Someone asked: "It may be granted that speaking constitutes a benefit through sound; however, since silence involves no speech, how can it be a benefit through sound? He replied:
"Silence is the absence of sound, yet it serves as a condition for speech, enabling people to obtain benefit; therefore, it too is a benefit through sound.

Regarding the Mahāyāna Sūtra on Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) that I have expounded, I have provisionally treated the matters of the Land of Ultimate Bliss according to the teachings of this Sahā world."
The meaning of these words truly encompasses the teachings proclaimed regarding the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
Regarding terms such as "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), they praise the Buddha’s exposition of the Pure Land Dharma-gate, which is both provisional and ultimate, and both ultimate and provisional;
within it, the underlying principles are not at all obscure. As for "perfect and sudden" (*yuantun*): "perfect" means complete and fully endowed; "sudden" means immediate.

"The mind is itself the Buddha. Regarding "the ultimate of the Perfect and Sudden" (*yuán-dùn zhī zhì*), this refers to the pinnacle of the Perfect and Sudden. It should be called "the Perfect and Sudden within the Perfect and Sudden.
As for the terms "definitive meaning" (*liǎo-yì*) and "Perfect and Sudden," they are all used with reduplication;

for example, the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are both teachings of definitive meaning and the Perfect and Sudden, yet both of these sutras praise the Dharma-gate of rebirth in the Pure Land. Is this not indeed [the case]?
Is this not the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) among all meanings, and the most perfect and sudden (*yuan-dun*) among all that is perfect and sudden?
If one attains rebirth by single-mindedly holding the Name for ten recitations or seven days, one immediately enters the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
What definitive, perfect, and sudden teaching could surpass this? As the Great Master Ciyun said, it is "the definitive meaning among definitive meanings" and "the Mahāyāna among Mahāyānas."
It is so. △ Third, the Sangha Jewel of the two lands, in two parts. First, the Bodhisattva Sangha:
"Miaode (Mañjuśrī), Puxian (Samantabhadra), Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara), Shizhi (Mahāsthāmaprāpta), and the assembly of the Pure Great Ocean.
The names of these great bodhisattvas such as Miaode have already been translated from Sanskrit into Chinese. If one were to now translate them from Chinese back into Sanskrit:
Thus, Miaode (Wondrous Virtue) is Mañjuśrī in the Sanskrit language; Puxian (Universal Goodness) is Samantabhadra in the Sanskrit language;
Guanzizai (Avalokiteśvara) is Avalokiteśvara in the Sanskrit language; and Shizhi (Powerful Attainment) is Mahāsthāmaprāpta in the Sanskrit language.

Miaode and Puxian serve as the left and right assistants to the Benevolent One (the Buddha), propagating his transformative teachings as his disciples. Guanyin and Shizhi serve as the attendants of Amitābha.
To his left and right were attendant disciples who were either followers of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or the Vaipulya sūtras,
as well as those for whom the Tathāgata had proclaimed the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, and the *Amitāyurdhyāna* sūtras.

During the recitation of the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Drum-Sound King Sūtra*, and other scriptures, there was no moment when the mallets and hammers did not strike one another, as the primary and accompanying elements were struck and raised to form the conditions for a pure Buddha-land and to gather the assembly destined for rebirth in that purity.
As it is with these Bodhisattvas here, so it is with those Great Beings there; they are like a sovereign and two ministers, whose movements and stillness are necessarily in accord.

Together with the assembly of the Pure Ocean, all of whom were pioneers of the Dharma-gates and eminent friends from the Lotus Pond—I prostrated and took refuge in every one of these jewels of the Sangha from the Western Land. Next, the Śrāvaka Saṃgha. (Question:

These masters are also great Bodhisattvas; why are they referred to as Śrāvakas? Answer: Because they maintain and transmit the Buddha-Dharma while manifesting the appearance of Śrāvakas, and because they cause all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way.)
Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Vasubandhu; here in this land, the patriarchs of the Lotus Society at Mount Lu, Tiantai Zhiyi, and Fazhi;
from antiquity to the present, these are the masters who propagated the Dharma.
Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa was the twelfth patriarch in the Western Heavens; he composed the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* to elucidate the practice of focused mindfulness.
The West is the most essential [region]. Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna was the fourteenth patriarch in the Western Heaven;
he was a native of South India who, within ninety days, mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and deeply penetrated the Dharma-patience (dharmakṣānti). He composed the *Mahākaruṇopāya-śāstra*.

He composed the *Mahā-vaiśāradya-śāstra*, as well as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. He frequently praised the Western Land and exhorted people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
There is a verse that says: "If a person aspires to become a Buddha, they should mindfully recite the name of Amitābha;

they shall immediately attain his manifestation before them. Therefore, I take refuge and pay homage. The school of this tradition venerates him as its founding patriarch. He was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
A native of Northern India, he composed treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and further authored the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-śāstra*.
He also produced verses for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land and the "Five-Gate" method of cultivation. Regarding the patriarchs of the Lotus Society (*Lian-she*), there were seven.

The first patriarch was the Dharma Master Huiyuan of the Jin dynasty; his secular surname was Jia, and he was a native of Yanmen. His learning encompassed both Confucianism and Daoism. At the age of...
At over twenty years of age, he met the Dharma Master Dao’an and, upon hearing him lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, attained a sudden and profound awakening.
He then remarked, "The divergent theories of the nine schools are all mere chaff. Later, he entered Mount Lu, where the Regional Inspector Huan Yi established Donglin Monastery for him to reside in.
For more than thirty years, his shadow never left the mountain. Whenever he escorted guests on excursions, he would always carry a tiger [skin].

The stream served as the boundary. At that time, monastics who had stilled their minds and lay believers who had severed worldly ties arrived without prior appointment, gathering from afar at the mere mention of his reputation;
together they numbered one hundred and twenty-three. They formed the Lotus Society (*Padmasaṃgha*), among whom eighteen individuals were particularly renowned for their fame.
Six times each day they performed prostrations and recitations with diligent perseverance, never retreating. Over ten years, they beheld the sacred countenance three times. Later, [at] Prajñā...

The platform was fixed and raised. He saw Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void of space. Within his circular halo were various transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance at his left and right.
He further saw the flowing water of light divided into fourteen branches, streaming upward and downward, proclaiming the doctrines of suffering and emptiness.
The Buddha said to Huiyuan: "By the power of my original vow, I have come to bring you peace."

I comfort you: seven days from now, you shall be reborn in my land. When the seven days had indeed passed, there appeared ten volumes of miscellaneous writings titled the *Lushan ji* (Collected Works of Mount Lu), which circulated widely in the world.
The details of these matters are found in his original biography; as the text is voluminous, it is not recorded here.
Huiyuan was truly the first in this land to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and is thus honored as the First Patriarch. The Second Patriarch was Shandao of Chang’an. His light...
Master Ming; the Third Patriarch, Nanyue Chengyuan, Dhyāna-master of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi; the Fourth Patriarch, Chang’an Fazhao, Dharma-master of the Five Assemblies;
the Fifth Patriarch, Xinting Shaokang, Dharma-master of the Terrace Grotto;
the Sixth Patriarch, Yongming Yanshou, Dharma-master Zhijue; the Seventh Patriarch, Zhaokong Shichang, Dharma-master Yuanjing; and Master Zhiyi.

His posthumous name was Zhiyi. He was a native of Huāróng and belonged to the secular surname Chén. At the time of his birth, there were numerous auspicious omens. At the age of seven, he entered Guòyuàn Monastery;
upon hearing the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) of the *Lotus Sūtra* being recited, he suddenly recalled it from memory as if it were something he had practiced in a previous life.
At fifteen, he prostrated before a Buddha image and vowed to renounce the world. At eighteen, he underwent the tonsure ceremony, and at twenty, he advanced to receive full ordination.
In the fifth year of the Tianjia era, he visited Master Huisi of Dasu Mountain in Guangzhou; the details of this are found in his biography and need not be recorded here in full.
He once composed a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* (the *Shiliu guan jing shu*) as well as the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*).
Later, before the Maitreya statue at Shicheng in eastern Shan, he had his disciples chant the title of the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* and admonished the assembly, saying: "Forty..."
The eight vows adorn the Pure Land. Though the fragrant terraces and jeweled trees are easy to reach, few go there;

yet even those who encounter the signs of the "fire chariot" (the karmic retribution for killing) can still attain rebirth if they repent in a single thought. How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and meditative concentration, and whose practice of the holy path is never in vain.
