the second phrase is "mind is identical with things"; and the third phrase is the mutual identity of mind and things, thereby establishing the three perfect and harmonious contemplations (*yuanrong san guan*).
The textual explanation is thus; however, what is valued is grasping the fundamental meaning. As for this fundamental meaning, it lies in what precedes.
Within the gateway of the single true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), that which is spoken of as "inherent nature" (*xingju*) refers precisely to the essence and magnitude of this nature.
For both mind and phenomena possess two meanings: being unchanging while following conditions (*suíyuán*), and following conditions while remaining unchanged.

If it were not for this inherent nature—the very essence and magnitude—how could one perceive the guiding compass of these three contemplations? Therefore, the mind possesses the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of an unchanging mind.

The mind created according to conditions refers to that which is produced by following conditions. As for "objects," there are objects within the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and there are objects produced through transformation according to conditions.
The mind of True Suchness is precisely that which is luminously pure and inherently pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm within the Single True Dharma-realm.
The mind created according to conditions refers to the gate of the mutual identity of mind and land, and the mutual identity of sense-faculties and sense-objects.

"Correct. It refers to a single moment of deluded mind. As for 'things within the nature of True Suchness,' this refers to the gate of the Single True Dharma-realm, which clarifies the ten realms inherently possessed by nature.

As for 'things created through following conditions,' this refers to the gate of the mutual identity of mind and land, which clarifies the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—created here in this land and in the Western Land, because they have True Suchness as their fundamental basis."
Because the capacity to possess and that which is possessed exist, there is the present day. The mind that transforms and creates according to conditions is precisely this deluded mind;

furthermore, there are things possessed and created by it. As for the things clarified in this present text, they are provisionally discussed in terms of the things intrinsically possessed within a single thought-moment.
When we reach the explanation below regarding the Pure Land—the environment and its inhabitants—which is the object of contemplation in this school, it is precisely this [intrinsic possession].
These are things created by the mind. If one does not understand this, how can one possibly resolve the textual passages concerning the two locations?
△ Next, the explanation and establishment of these two points consists of two parts: first, clarifying the mastery over the general and the particular.
Therefore, when contemplating the environment and the inhabitants of the Land of Ultimate Bliss,

it is entirely appropriate to take the three contemplations of our own mind to illuminate the three truths of that single realm; it is likewise entirely appropriate to take the single mind of the three contemplations of our own mind to illuminate that single realm of the three truths.

What was explained in the preceding text all involved contemplating the Buddha through the mind itself as a provisional contemplation. Now, however, one relies upon an objective realm to cultivate contemplation as a concrete object;
this is the primary intent of the present treatise. It is what is meant in the *Miaozongchao* (The Sublime Commentary) when it says:

"Based upon the nature of the mind, one contemplates that which is the environment and its inhabitants (*ni-sheng*). When the environment and inhabitants are easily manifested, one relies upon that environment and its inhabitants to contemplate the nature of the mind. Mind...

This is precisely what is meant by "the nature is easily manifested. When one contemplates my mind through the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to illuminate that single object (*ālambana*) of the three truths (*tisraḥ satya*), the mind is fundamentally one;
how could this not be a single contemplation? Nevertheless, it does not preclude the fact that within this one there are three.
The object is fundamentally one; how could this not be a single object? Yet, it likewise does not preclude the fact that within this one there are three.
This refers to using the three contemplations of a single mind to contemplate the three truths of a single object; this is what emerges from the ordinary.
However, when one uses the single mind of the three contemplations of one's own mind to illuminate that single object of the three truths, this differs from the ordinary.
It is by means of the three contemplations within a single mind that [the practitioner] binds them together as emptiness, and the three truths within a single object.

To unify these as a single bundle is termed the "Provisional" (假). To unify the object and the contemplation as one is termed the "Middle" (中). This makes it easy for people to practice and cultivate;
it can be called grasping the essential core of the teachings of the Mountain School (Shan-jiao) and attuning to the life-vein of the Tathāgata.
△ Next, the proof of the threefold perfect contemplation (yuanrong san guan).
The Great Master of Huxi said: "The objective realm is the wondrous provisional, and contemplation is emptiness. When both realm and contemplation are forgotten, this is the Middle Way.
How could forgetting and illumination ever have a sequence of before and after? When the single mind is fused and severed, it leaves no trace. How could the three contemplations not be thus?"
Regarding the object as the "wondrous provisional": this refers to what the verses of the Youmen (Gate of Existence) call the "inconceivable provisional," which is not a partial provisional.

Rather, it takes the single realm of the three truths as the wondrous provisional. Regarding contemplation as "emptiness": this refers to what is called "true emptiness that is not empty" and is not merely empty.
Rather, it takes the single mind of the three contemplations as the contemplation of emptiness. The simultaneous forgetting of both object and contemplation is precisely the Middle Way.
What is called "perfectly complete within the perfect" refers not merely to the Middle Way, but to the three objects and the three contemplations.

Taking the nature of the mind, which is free from all dependence, as the Middle Contemplation; and since forgetting and illuminating are never sequential, the two contemplations of Emptiness and Provisionality constitute simultaneous illumination, while the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way constitutes simultaneous forgetting.
Thus, Emptiness and Provisionality are identical with the Middle, and the Middle is identical with Emptiness and Provisionality—this is forgetting.
Whether it be forgetting or illuminating, all is unified within the single mind. What sequence or priority could there be? Therefore it is said:

"The single mind is fused and absolute, utterly without succession. To say "without succession" means that both forgetting and illuminating are simultaneously extinguished and simultaneously severed; thus, there is no succession.

The final sentence concludes with the principle of *dharmatā*. That is to say, when one can understand in this way and cultivate in this way, the wondrous contemplation of non-action occurs spontaneously;
there is nowhere that it is not present.

△ Next, regarding the three gates that discuss the excellence [of the fruit], there are two parts. First, one gate clarifies the mutual intersection of the arising of sentient beings and the Buddha-way.
Second, two gates clarify that there is no separation in terms of time or place. Within the first of these, there are two sections; first is the heading.
Eight, the Gate of Spontaneous Response:
Sentient beings invoking the name and recollecting the Buddha constitute the "stimulus" (*gan*); the Buddhas receiving and guiding them toward rebirth constitutes the "response" (*ying*).

Because the natures of the Buddhas and sentient beings are interrelated, this occurs spontaneously; hence it is called "spontaneous" (*renyun*). △ Next, the explanation of the two [aspects], first: the description.
The verse establishes the thesis: My mind moves the Buddhas; Amitābha responds from afar. Their natures are naturally related, like a magnet attracting a needle.
The first line clarifies the movement (of the mind); the second line clarifies the response; the third line clarifies the subtlety of this movement and response; the fourth line provides a simile.

To manifest this. △ Second, the interpretation of the meaning according to the school, which has two parts: first, a general clarification of sentient beings and Buddhas; second, the explanation that establishes this school. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, clarifying the nature of heaven (the Buddha-nature); second, clarifying response and resonance. Within the first of these, there are again two: first, clarifying that sentient beings and Buddhas share the same source; second, the formal clarification.
Within the first of these, there are two: first, the formal clarification.
The Commentary states: All Buddhas and sentient beings share the same source of awakening. Although delusion and enlightenment differ, their principle remains eternally equal.
The first two phrases clarify the fundamental principle of sentient beings and Buddhas; the third phrase clarifies the phenomenal characteristics of ascent and descent.

From the standpoint of phenomenal characteristics, they cannot help but be different; from the standpoint of rational nature, they cannot help but be the same. If one says that the phenomenal is identical to the fundamental principle...
Regarding phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): the entirety of phenomena constitutes the fundamental principle (*tattva*). Although they are differentiated, they are without differentiation.
Therefore, it is said that although delusion and enlightenment differ, the principle remains eternally equal. △ Next, the citation of scriptural proof.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas are the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings; sentient beings are the sentient beings within the minds of the Buddhas.
To fully exhaust this principle, one must explain it by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), as has already been clarified above.
Next, we clarify that the mind and its functions penetrate one another.
Speaking from this perspective, the subtle essence of the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings is never at any time not in communication. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"When the subtle essence of the mind is in communication, it is profoundly still (*zhanran*) in its very place. This refers to the practitioner who has perfectly subdued the three delusions;

their subtle essence of the mind during the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is in communication with the ultimate subtle essence of the minds of all Buddhas, such that they flow together without obstruction.
Yet there is no trace; they merge into a single essence. Thus, in their respective places, they are serene and still.

Now, based on the fact that the fundamental nature of the Buddha and the principle-nature of sentient beings are identical, they are never not in communication [yǒng-huì]. Though identical, they are not identical; one must skillfully distinguish this.
Next, clarifying response and resonance (gǎnyìng). Part One: Clarifying through negation that without resonance there is no response. Sub-part One: Resolving doubts.
It is simply that while the Buddhas never have a moment when they do not wish to deliver sentient beings, those beings, in every thought-moment, remain deluded and turn their backs on them.

Some may raise this doubt: "If we sentient beings are constantly in intimate communion with the minds of the Buddhas, then in our daily lives we should see the Buddhas from time to time, and at the end of our lives we should each attain rebirth in their pure lands. Yet now, we neither see them nor [attain such rebirth]."
Wherein lies the meaning of "penetrating" (*tōng*)? Therefore, the Master of the Treatise explains the doubt (as follows).
It is because the natures of all Buddhas and sentient beings are similar that there is never a time when they do not wish to deliver sentient beings;

yet, because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings and those of the Buddhas are distant, sentient beings moment by moment remain deluded and turn their backs on them. △ Next, he provides an analogy.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Shi-zhi said: "One person focuses exclusively on recollection; another focuses exclusively on forgetting. Thus, they may encounter what they do not encounter, or see what they do not see.
One who focuses exclusively on recollection is like the Buddhas, who at no time do not wish to deliver sentient beings. One who focuses exclusively on forgetting is like the multitudes."

From birth, sentient beings are deluded and turn their backs on [the Buddha]. Because the Buddha desires to deliver them, when they encounter or see him, because they have turned their backs through delusion from birth, they do not encounter or see him.
△ Next, the main section clarifying that there is a response whenever there is a stimulus, in two parts.
First, the analogy and application regarding the mutual remembrance between mother and child. First, the analogy.
If you, my son, remember your mother as she remembers you, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall never be separated or far apart.
If you, my son, remember your mother, it is like sentient beings recollecting the Buddha. "As she remembers you" means that recollecting the Buddha should be intimate and earnest;
it should not be superficial or perfunctory. To recollect with superficiality is like a child's remembrance that is not focused; it will certainly [fail].

It should be like a mother remembering her child—there is no place where she does not think of him, and no time when she does not mind him. This serves as an analogy for the mind that recollects the Buddha:

throughout the three periods of time and across the ten directions, there is nowhere it does not contemplate in accordance with the nature of reality, nor anywhere it does not illuminate beyond all limitations.
If one can truly act in this way, then the Buddha-mother gives birth to the child; from birth to birth, they shall not be separated or distant.

Although this section clarifies the mutual resonance of the path between the response and the stimulus, it actually accords with the single thought-moment of the beginning and the source. May students understand this. △ Next, the synthesis.
If sentient beings, in their minds, recollect the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; they will not be far from the Buddha.
"Recollecting the Buddha" (yìfó) is spoken of in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), while "contemplating the Buddha" (niànfó) should be discussed in terms of principle (*tattva*).

In terms of phenomena, every thought-moment takes the pure realm as its object; in terms of principle, every moment of mindfulness accords with the original source. Thus, these are the sixteen supreme [recollections].
Contemplate the objects of perception in their proper sequence; with single-mindedness, employ the threefold contemplation to illuminate them in perfect fusion.
If one can maintain such mindfulness, the Buddha will be seen in this very life. Upon casting off this body, one will certainly attain the stages of realization in future lives.

Indeed, such a person bears the entire burden of the Way and is not far removed from the Buddha. Next, the conclusion and exhortation regarding the efficacy of the practice and its basis in one's innate nature.
It is precisely because of this equality of the single principle and the mutual connection of their natures that [the Buddhas] are able to spontaneously extract suffering and bestow happiness.
Regarding the equality of the single principle: the three natures of sentient beings and the three bodies of the Buddhas are non-dual.

Regarding the mutual connection of their natures: this borrows worldly phenomena as an analogy; Heaven, through the Yin and Yang and the Five Elements, transforms and gives birth to the myriad things.
All things belong to the same category of vital energy (*qi*). Therefore, it is said that heaven and earth constitute one great cosmos, and the human body constitutes a small cosmos.
When a father transmits [his essence] to his son, he likewise uses his own small cosmos to transform and give birth to his son.
The large and the small share the same energy; father and son share the same form; their bones and blood correspond, and their karmic types summon one another. This is the nature of Heaven.
This is also relevant. The Way of sentient beings and Buddhas is likewise so. They share the same essential nature and originate from a single source of awakening.
This is like the way in which the nature of Heaven is inherently interconnected. The compassion of all Buddhas constantly desires to bestow joy and extract suffering;

if there is an occasion for resonance and invocation, they immediately manifest their response. All of this occurs spontaneously and naturally; therefore, it is called "acting according to conditions" (*renyun*). △ Next, the explanation is completed.
This school has four [sections]. First, it clarifies that Amitābha’s wondrous response is already perfected;
how much more so for the Buddha of Immeasurable Life! In the causal stage, he made forty-eight vows, vowing to take up the Land of Ultimate Bliss and to gather in sentient beings.
Now, his path and its fruit have long been accomplished, and his saṃnāha (armor of resolve) has long been fulfilled.
The vows and compassion of all Buddhas are indeed equal; nevertheless, there are those that are general and those that are urgent, and there are those that are intimate and those that are distant.
The preceding explanation of the extraction from suffering and the bestowal of happiness was based on their innate nature, showing generally that no Buddha is without this quality.
However, speaking in terms of their specific vows, the Buddhas' relation to the sentient beings of this Sahā world is general and distant; it is only...

I, Śākyamuni, and Amitābha were brothers-in-arms during our causal stages. Out of particular compassion for the Sahā world, Śākyamuni was born into the evil age of the five turbidities to subdue those who are stubborn and fierce;
Amitābha appeared in the pure, peaceful, and blissful land to gather in and harmonize those who are compliant.
It is like a stern father and a compassionate mother who both shape and nurture their child until the path of transformation is perfected. This is indeed the work of the Bodhisattvas...
Although the Great Compassion of all Buddhas is equal, there are differences in the opening and closing of their vows. When condensed, they consist solely of the Four Great Vows;
when expanded, the variations in number are not uniform. Thus, the Medicine Master Buddha expands them into twelve, while Dharmākara expands them into forty-eight.
Nevertheless, while in the causal stage, one merely gives rise to the *saṃnāha* (armor) of resolve at the initial moment of mind; now, Amitābha abides in the state of fruition.
Thus, in the end, Great Compassion rushes to the rescue; the wondrous response is already established, and the wondrous resonance thus arrives.
Therefore, the compassion of Amitābha is both urgent and intimate. △ Second, the exhortation for sentient beings to establish the wondrous resonance has two parts.
First, the exhortation not to doubt.
Therefore, all sentient beings should not worry that the Buddha will not come to respond to them.

Among those in the world who practice *nien-fo*, the greatest source of anxiety and doubt is this: "Even though I now practice *nien-fo* and seek rebirth [in the Pure Land], what if the Buddha does not come to welcome and guide me at the moment of death?
Would my efforts not then be in vain? For this reason, it is exhorted: "All who practice *nien-fo*, do not..."
One should not feel anxiety, for the natures of sentient beings and Buddhas are interrelated, and because Amitābha’s vows have been fulfilled.
Next, I exhort you to establish your resolve:
simply cultivate faith and mindfulness, and repeatedly make the vow to be born in the Western Land.
Those in the world who do not rejoice in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land fall into three general errors: first, lack of faith;
second, lack of mindfulness; and third, lack of aspiration. Regarding the first, lack of faith, there are many categories, but roughly speaking, there are three types.
The first is total lack of faith; this is found among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The second is to believe only in one's own Buddha while disbelieving in other Buddhas;

this is found among practitioners of meditation (*dhyāna*). The third is to believe in other Buddhas while disbelieving in one's own Buddha; this is found among those who practice according to ritual forms (*sāṃketika-yogin*).

Now, the Master of the Treatise exhorts people that they must have faith in both their own and other Buddhas; through this, they will realize that there is no distinction between living beings and Buddhas.
Second: There are three types of non-recollection (*amanasikāra*). First, total non-recollection; this is found among ordinary, indolent worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, recollecting oneself but not others; this is found among practitioners of meditation (*dhyāyin*). Third, recollecting others but not oneself;
this is found among those concerned with phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Now, the Master of the Treatise exhorts people that one must [practice] both self and other together.
"Mindfulness. This is the realization that mindfulness is non-mindfulness. Regarding the third [category], non-aspiration, there are also three types.

First is total non-aspiration, which is found among ordinary, indolent worldlings. Second is the aspiration to become a Buddha oneself, without aspiring to be gathered and perfected by another Buddha;
this is found among practitioners of dhyāna. Third is the aspiration for another Buddha to come and welcome one, while remaining unaware that one's own Buddha is already present.
[The text] proceeds. Such characteristics exist among people; now the Master exhorts that one must wish for both oneself and others.
This realization is that birth is itself non-birth. △ Third, an analogy for the spontaneous resonance between the Buddha and sentient beings.
It is like a magnet and a needle, which attract one another spontaneously.
A magnet is a "mother-stone" (*māṇikya*); the magnet is the mother of iron, and iron is the child of the magnet.
Even among insentient things, there is a natural affinity and a mutual resonance of their elemental constituents; this occurs spontaneously and without the need for effort.
This serves as a metaphor for Amitābha’s unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), which acts as a compassionate mother to all sentient beings;

it is that in which the path of resonance and response intersects without the slightest error. △ Fourth, clarifying the ease or difficulty of the resonance between the living being and the Buddha, in three parts. First, borrowing a metaphor to examine whether the resonance is harmonious or not.
However, while a magnet can attract iron, it cannot attract copper; and while a needle can align with a magnet, it cannot align with jade.
In this analogy, copper and jade are used as examples for the distant and the proximate, respectively. The application of these metaphors to the actual meaning is quite clear.
Next, the application to the Dharma [the vows] is related to the aspiration.
It is like how a Buddha can deliver those with whom he has a karmic connection, yet cannot deliver those without such a connection.
Sentient beings are easily moved by Amitābha, but not so easily moved by other Buddhas; is this not because the vows of the sentient beings and the Buddha are mutually related?
The Buddha can deliver those with whom he has a karmic affinity, but cannot deliver those without such affinity. It is like a magnet that can attract iron but cannot attract copper.
Sentient beings find it easy to respond to Amitābha, yet difficult to respond to other Buddhas. It is like a needle that can adhere to a magnet, but cannot adhere to jade.
Now, Amitābha Buddha and our Śākyamuni were themselves among the sixteen [sons] of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
Since his time as a prince, he has constantly remained in this Sahā world out of compassion for sentient beings.

His vows of loving-kindness and pity are profound; those with whom he has formed karmic connections are numerous; the duration of his practice to fulfill his vows is long; his mastery in gathering a Buddha-land is supreme; his mindfulness of sentient beings is earnest;
and the application of his supernormal powers is vast. That his natural affinity is thus established is no small matter. △
The three fetters (saṃyojana) manifest that one must possess the three essentials.
Thus, for those seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, the triad of faith, practice, and aspiration—none of which may be lacking—is indispensable.
This triad of faith, practice, and aspiration is called the "three essentials of rebirth. "Essentials" means that which is urgent and necessary; it signifies that these three are all...
Rebirth [in the Pure Land] is of vital importance; one must not be lax for even a moment. It is like the collar of a garment or the hem of a skirt:
by grasping the collar, the garment comes with it; by lifting the hem, the skirt follows. For practice cannot be established without faith, and faith cannot be perfected without practice.
These two methods lack any other wish or constraint. Faith is likened to the tilting of a boat’s bow, while practice is like the boat itself.
The bulwarks and oars; may they be like the stern and rudder of a ship. When these three are all complete, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.
△ Next, two sections clarify that there is no separation by time or place. The first section discusses the excellence regarding place;
the second section discusses the excellence regarding time. Within the first, there are two parts: first, the heading.

9. "The two are eternally one" means that "that" refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and "this" refers to the Sahā world. Although these two differ in being pure or defiled, they do not exist outside of the single thought-moment of the person themselves;
therefore, they are called "eternally one. △ Next, the explanation has two parts. First, the verse is cited to establish the thesis.

If a person, at the time of death, is able to maintain right mindfulness—whether seeing light or flowers—and has already attained rebirth in a jeweled pond, their pure karma will have been perfected within a single lifetime.
Right mindfulness governs the moment of departure; as the ancients said, "If one maintains right mindfulness during ordinary life, how could it fail to be present at the end?
This describes those who attain the highest level. As for those whose minds are distracted during their ordinary lives...
To invoke the Buddha and, at the moment of death, gather the distracted mind back into meditative concentration—this is what is attained by those of middling capacity.

For ordinary, ignorant, and even wicked or rebellious sentient beings, to be exhorted by virtuous friends toward the correct path—this is what is attained by those of inferior capacity. Such is the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
It need not be so in every case. It is sufficient that at the moment of death one’s single thought returns to the correct state;

then, whether in the Lotus Pond or the Nine Grades, one shall all participate in the Dharma-stream. However, there are those who, despite maintaining right mindfulness, have no perception whatsoever as their consciousness is entrusted to a lotus flower;

furthermore, there are those whose karma drags them into the dark realm where their rebirth is adjudicated—these cases are not discussed here. Now, it is clarified that the two states are eternally one and the same, being correct.

In this land, at the moment of death, one beholds light and flowers; having already received birth by transformation within the jeweled ponds of that land, were it not for constant and singular [practice], how could such wondrousness be attained?
△ Second, the interpretation of the meaning according to the school has three parts. First, establishing the foundation by means of empirical evidence regarding phenomena.
The Treatise says: According to the *Shengzhuan* (Biographies of Rebirth), Zhang Kang served as a Hanlin Academician under the Shi Jin dynasty.

He recited the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times, vowing to be reborn in the Western Pure Land. One day, while suffering from illness, he focused solely on the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he said to his family members:
The Western Pure Land is located right to the west of the hall. Amitābha Buddha sits upon a lotus flower.
[The monk] saw the old man’s grandson playing and prostrating on the golden sand of the lotus pond. After a long while, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away.
The old man’s grandson was the son of Kang.

Zhang Kang was a person who aspired for rebirth in the Pure Land. He recited the Great Compassion Mantra to point toward the practices and vows for rebirth, and he focused solely on chanting the Buddha’s name to indicate the source of right mindfulness.
This is because, when beset by the sufferings of death, one has no leisure to recite mantras; only the Buddha’s name is easy to apply.
It is easily established as right mindfulness; that is to say, it refers to the speech of family members. This clearly demonstrates the verification that self and other are eternally one.
As for those who suspect this to be the work of Māra, it is entirely because they do not understand the principle of the Pure Land being Mind-only.
Someone may ask: "The lotus flowers you see are the signs of the Pure Land; if the old man and the child are also within them, does this mean the child has been born [there]?"
"Is he dead? If he is dead, he possesses no karma or vows; how then can he be reborn there? If he is reborn, how could he dwell together with ordinary people in the Lotus Realm?
None of these [objections] hold true. He replied: "Another version of the text records that the father’s son died at the age of three."
Or they may be those who have returned from there; their past vows were already fulfilled, and they have cast off this remaining life to take rebirth in that land.
Or it may be because they inherit the power of the ancestral prayers and aspirations. As a sutra states:

"If one merely catches the wind from the body of a mantra-holder or the water used to bathe them, one can still attain rebirth; how much more so for those who personally receive the power of such prayers and aspirations?"
Ah! △ Next, by means of the nature of mind, the duality of subject and object is dissolved. This clarifies that the land resides within the mind.
Why is this so? It is because the Western World of Ultimate Bliss is but one land within my own mind;
the Sahā world is likewise but one land within my own mind.
The explanation of Master Zhang Kang’s signs of rebirth establishes the principle that this world and that world are eternally one.

Although the Sahā world and Sukhāvatī differ in being impure and pure respectively, the mind capable of possessing them does not differ between the two. △ Next, it clarifies that the mind has no distance or proximity.

Speaking in terms of lands, there are hundreds of thousands of billions of distinctions between this and that; yet observing from the perspective of the mind, fundamentally there is neither distance nor proximity.

Speaking in terms of lands, they are distinct because they manifest the totality of nature as form; speaking in terms of the mind, they are identical because they embody the totality of form as nature.
They are constantly divided yet constantly united. Whether they appear as different or as the same, it is permissible to maintain them as such.
It is permissible even to lose it. How much more so when the mind itself is fully endowed with the three natures, vast and pure;

what distinction, then, can there be between this and that, or between purity and defilement? △ Third, regarding the aspect of the fruit, cutting off coming and going, in three parts: first, resolving objections.
However, since sentient beings have first taken birth, they have been confined by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), failing to accord with the source of the mind that is true nature.
Some may raise this objection: "The Pure Land is but the mind; who does not possess it? It can be seen right now before one's eyes—why wait until the moment of death?
To explain this: since taking birth, there are those whose time is long and those whose time is short; there are those whose confinement of true nature is shallow and those whose is deep.

"Deep" refers to the beginningless past when distant, and to this present life when near; it refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) when shallow, and to all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) when deep.
For now, let us proceed generally by taking this present life as the domain of the aggregate of form. Why is it that this true nature is confined here and fails to accord with the source of the mind?

It is because among those who transmigrate, the ordinary are many and the sages are few; while dwelling on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is difficult to shatter the aggregates. Now...
Discussing the five sense organs horizontally: they are all obscured by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Therefore, seeing does not transcend form, and hearing does not go beyond sound;
even when the eyes and ears are at a distance, they fail to see or hear. This is called the "limited nature" of true reality, which fails to accord with the source of the mind.
△ Next, the correct explanation.

When the karmic fruition of one who practices mindfulness of the Buddha reaches maturity, and they are about to relinquish the present aggregate and proceed toward the aggregate of rebirth, a lotus flower in the Pure Land suddenly appears before them.
This is a realm of mind-only, devoid of any characteristics of coming or going, or of self and other.

The first two lines clarify the accomplishment of pure karma. The next two lines clarify rebirth according to that karma. The following two lines clarify the destruction of the seal and the formation of the inscription.
The subsequent three lines use the principle of "mind-only" to dissolve delusive appearances.

Since it says, "when about to cast off the present aggregate and proceed toward the aggregate of birth," it is clear that the five aggregates have not yet been destroyed. As for "the lotus flower appearing before one," this refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Although stubborn delusions have not yet been shattered, as this illusory body is about to depart, the eyes will no longer be confined by forms and the ears will no longer be confined by sounds;
then, lands of hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis* away will suddenly appear before one.
All of these are the realm of mind-only. How could there be any characteristics of coming and going, or of self and other, to be apprehended?
△ Third, citing scriptural evidence, in two parts. First, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "At the time of the end of life, before warmth and tactile sensation have been relinquished, the good and evil of one's entire life appear simultaneously."
They appear instantaneously. If one’s thoughts are purely contemplative, one will immediately fly upward and will certainly be reborn in the heavens.

If within that flying mind there is a combination of merit, wisdom, and pure vows, the mind will naturally open, and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the pure lands; according to one’s vows, one shall be reborn therein.
When a person receives birth, it is formed through the conjunction of consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*).

As the Sūtra says, at the moment when one is about to die but has not yet died—when the warmth and tactile sensation have not yet been abandoned, and at the juncture when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to be relinquished but has not yet been relinquished—the good and evil deeds performed throughout one’s life manifest all at once.
If evil prevails, one falls with pure emotion; if goodness prevails, one ascends with pure thought.

As for "flying": when one cultivates both good and evil in a mixed manner, the ascent and descent of one's emotional thoughts occur simultaneously. The characteristics of this are very clear as explained in the sutras.
Regarding those who fly with a mind that possesses both merit and wisdom: merit assists in cultivation, while wisdom consists of mindfulness of the Buddha; together they constitute pure karma.
Furthermore, for those who add the making of vows to seek rebirth there, their minds will naturally open.
One beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions and is reborn in all pure lands according to one’s vows; this is because the primary cause—the relinquishing of form—is not obstructed.

By analogy with this, even if one is submerged in a state of mind that slanders the Triple Gem and harbors evil aspirations, one will inevitably find the mind opened naturally, seeing King Yama and all the hells, and through the relinquishing of form, will be reborn according to one’s vows.
Because they are in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), beings in the intermediate state all attain the five supernormal powers; this is precisely due to this reason.

Next, regarding the *Myōshū* (Exquisite Commentary), Master Hōchi said: "One must know that at the point of death, when one sees oneself sitting upon a golden lotus, this is already the *upapattibhava* (birth-body) of that land.
This also refers to this same meaning.
The Great Master Tiantai’s *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "When he closed his eyes and reached the end, he leaped upward to the precious terrace;
as the inscription was completed and the seal destroyed, he sat upon a golden lotus and attained birth through transformation. The first phrase is easily understood.

Regarding the second phrase, "the inscription was completed and the seal destroyed," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-seven, says: "It is like a wax seal pressed into clay; the seal and the clay meet."

The seal vanishes and the inscription appears; this serves as a metaphor for the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), whose present aggregates (*skandha*) perish and the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arise.

The Great Master Fazhi said: "I now borrow this passage to illustrate the Bodhisattva who is reborn [in the Pure Land]: here in this land the aggregates perish, and there in that land the aggregates arise.
One must know that at the moment of death, seeing oneself seated upon a golden lotus flower is already the arising of the aggregates of birth in that land."
...so it is. △ Next, the first section discusses the "Excellence" (miao) in terms of time, in two parts.
First, the heading: The Section on the Mutual Presence of the Ten [Dharmas] in the Present and Future.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "That which arises at the very moment of birth is simultaneously subject to extinction; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. Therefore, it is said in the teachings:

Nine ages within a single kṣaṇa; three thousand worlds within one thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*). It is further said: "The ten ages of past and present—beginning and end—are never separate from the present moment.
Moreover, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.
These all express the principle that the past and future mutually contain one another. △ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the statement of the verse establishes the thesis.
The practitioner who now recollects the Buddha’s merits will not be in vain; the fruit already exists within the cause, like a lotus flower in full bloom.
The first two lines clarify that for one who recollects the Buddha, their merit is never wasted; the third line explains the reason why this is so.
The fourth phrase is illustrated by means of a metaphor. △ Next, the explanation of the meaning according to the school (*zong*) has two parts. First, clarifying that the fruit is produced by causes.
The Treatise says: "Those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching suddenly awaken to the nature of the mind; they practice without practicing, cultivating that Land of Bliss within their own nature."
That which is fully possessed as ultimate bliss is manifested through cultivation.

Now, while the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is the same for all, the teachings are distinguished as partial (*prādeśika*) or perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). As for the inclusion of gradual and sudden merit, these are differentiated solely by whether there is awakening or no awakening, and whether it is perfect or not perfect;
it is by this that the gradual and the sudden are distinguished. Herein, we clarify the person of the perfect-sudden teaching, who from the very beginning is sudden.

Awaken to the nature of the mind: the arising of the mind is itself the Buddha-mind. Because its source transcends the ocean of fruits, when one awakens to the mind’s inherent completeness, there is no dharma that is not complete;
when one awakens to the measure of its nature, there is no land it does not pervade; when one awakens to the essence of its nature, there is neither birth nor extinction.

Having awakened to this, one should rightly proceed with cultivation. Yet, though one cultivates, one remains fully aware that there is nothing to cultivate—this is cultivation within non-cultivation.
Cultivating that Land of Bliss: although it is inherently possessed within one's nature, its entirety remains obscured by delusion.

If one does not practice with perfect completeness, then the inherent Ultimate Bliss will never be manifested. Therefore, those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching call this the "Sublime Practice of Non-action."

△ Second, the explanation of the mutual identity of cause and effect, in two parts: first, the mutual identity explained in terms of inherent nature; second, the mutual identity explained in terms of the essence of that nature.
Within the first part, there are three sections. First, establishing the fundamental basis.

This nature of mind vertically penetrates the three periods of time and horizontally encompasses the ten directions of space. The Buddha-dharma, the dharma of arising, the True Dharma, the dharma of reliance, the causal dharma, and the resultant dharma are all perfectly accomplished within a single thought-moment.
This "nature of mind" refers to that which was suddenly awakened to above; vertically it penetrates the three periods of time, speaking in terms of the essence of the nature;

horizontally it encompasses the ten directions of space, speaking in terms of the magnitude of the nature; and it includes the Buddha-dharma and the dharmas of sentient beings, speaking in terms of the inherent completeness of the nature.

The Buddha-dharma is the Buddha-realm (*buddhadhātu*). The dharmas of birth-and-death are the nine realms. The True Dharma (*saddharma*) refers to the one thousand [realms] of the true reality (*dharmatā*).

The Dharma according to phenomena refers to the one thousand [realms] of the land. All of the above are spoken in terms of the "identity-in-principle" (*li-ji*). The Dharma of causes is spoken in terms of the four identities beginning with "name" (*ming-zi-ji*).
The Dharma of the fruit is spoken in terms of the "ultimate identity" (*jiong-jing-ji*). These six kinds of judging identity do not depart from the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*).

Although that which is encompassed by these faculties is manifold, when the present sense organs and their objects encounter one another, the mind arises and is perfectly accomplished in a single thought-moment.
Is it not marvelous how the phenomena of sentient beings and the phenomena of the mind are thus unified? △ Next, the explanation is established.
Therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are said to "arise cultivation from the entirety of nature" and to have "the entirety of cultivation reside within nature.
Although "arising cultivation from the entirety of nature" is termed the cause, because "the entirety of cultivation resides within nature," the fruit is present within the cause.
Since the causal dharmas possessed and the resultant dharmas possessed coexist within a single nature, the mind-nature is interfused and there is no dharma that is not encompassed.

For those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha—encompassing all ordinary beings and those on the causal stages, whether they have attained awakening or not—whatever cultivation they undertake is termed "cultivation arising entirely from nature" (quán xìng qǐ xiū) and "cultivation existing entirely within nature" (quán xiū zài xìng).

This is because the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), which is unchanging, is able to function as the "function according to conditions" (suíyuán zhī yòng) by responding to defiled or pure conditions. Although there is a difference between those who have awakened and those who have not, its unchanging [nature remains the same].
In essence, they are one. Now, those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) have already opened the perfect understanding; they are able to realize that this entire nature gives rise to cultivation.

Speaking in terms of cultivation, it is called the cause; speaking in terms of the nature, wherein the entirety of cultivation resides within the nature, how could this not mean that the fruit exists within the cause?
By means of the "causal factors" and so forth possessed [within the nature], the principle that "the fruit exists within the cause" is explained. This refers to what is possessed.
The causal dharma is the nine realms inherently possessed by nature; the resultant dharma possessed therein is the Buddha realm inherently possessed by nature.
Since these both coexist within a single mind, the nature of the mind is pervasive and interfused, such that there is no dharma not subsumed and no dharma not directed toward.

Therefore, the cause of sentient beings in this Sahā world reciting the Buddha’s name already possesses the nine grades of fruition in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. △ Third, the illustration through analogy.
Thus, it is like a lotus flower in full bloom, within which there is fruit.

The two characters "Miaofa" (Wondrous Dharma) in the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* take the lotus flower as a metaphor. The Tathāgata’s establishment of the doctrine is profoundly deep, and Tiantai’s esoteric exposition is exceedingly extensive;
yet, to speak briefly, this serves as a comprehensive metaphor for both the provisional (trace) and the fundamental (original), referring to the two gates of the trace and the original. Each...
There are three metaphors; here we take only the blooming lotus flower as a metaphor for the cause of the complete awakening of nature through cultivation by means of mindfulness of the Buddha.
The fruit within the flower serves as a metaphor for the fruit of the nine grades of cultivation being fully present within nature. Flower and fruit exist simultaneously.
It is simply that cultivation and nature are non-dual. △ Next, the clarification of the essence of nature has three parts. First, the heading:

Furthermore, this mind is eternally abiding, without arising or ceasing, coming or going; the very mind that recites the Buddha’s name now is precisely the moment of receiving birth in the Lotus Pond in the future.

Previously, it was clarified that the nature and its attributes are mutually identical; although there were statements regarding their vertical pervasiveness and horizontal omnipresence, the primary intent lay in the inherent presence of all within the nature (*xingju*).
Now, we shall explicitly clarify the essence of the nature (*xingtǐ*), while also concurrently addressing the magnitude of the nature (*xingliang*).
Since this mind of nianfo is eternally abiding and devoid of arising and ceasing, or coming and going, is it not the case that this very present mind of nianfo is itself the [Buddha]?
This is the fruit of receiving birth within the Lotus Pond. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In a single thought-moment, universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. These words may serve as verification. △ Next, the evidence.
Therefore, it is said that for one who has first resolved their mind [for enlightenment], the lotus seed has already sprouted within the precious pond of Sukhāvatī.

If they practice with diligence and do not regress, it will grow day by day until the flower gradually unfolds; according to their merit, it will blaze with brilliance in varying degrees. Should they, however, become lax, regress, or be muddled by remorse, it will gradually wither away.
If they can renew themselves, the flower will once again become fresh and radiant; if this does not occur, the sprout will scorch and the seed perish.

Thus, the commentator cites this incident as a scriptural verification.

Specifically, in the *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Rebirth), it is recorded that during his meditative concentration, Dharma Master Biancai of Leifeng traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and beheld an exceptionally beautiful flower. He asked about it, saying, "It awaits Neti."
Regarding Master Ben, Master Xi of Zifu Temple said: "In my meditative absorption, I saw golden lotus flowers; people say these were to await Master Ben.
I also saw countless lotus flowers and asked about them, saying they were to await those who would receive ordination.
Some of the flowers were withered, and it was said these were people who had regressed and fallen away. △ Third, the conclusion.
Furthermore, regarding these lotus flowers: who planted them? That they exist both in the present and the future has a definitive meaning.
The lotus flowers of this Sahā world are planted by the hand; because form gives rise to form, and the physical body depends on conditions, their mutual distance is near.
Yet, though they seem near, they are actually far. The lotus flowers of the Pure Land are planted by the mind. By...
The mind attains the mind. Since the nature of the mind has no dependence, they appear far apart; yet though they seem distant, they are in fact near.

Since the fruit exists within the cause in the mind, and its nature pervades horizontally and exhausts vertically, the marks of coming and going are obliterated and the forms of mutual dependence are severed.
That the present and the future exist interdependently leaves no room for doubt.

At this time, Zen Master Jian Xueping of Tianquan Temple in Wukang, Wuxing, having previously explored the lineage of Shaoshi and investigated the matter within his own person, has already attained a state of preeminence. Later, he heard from...
The various patriarchs of antiquity all extensively propagated the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha; he yearned for this with all his heart.

In the autumn of the Year of Yi-hai, he came to Lingfeng Peak with his mind fixed upon this aspiration. While on the road, he clearly beheld the sacred countenance of the Buddha who Welcomes and Leads.

Upon reaching the mountain and prostrating before the image of Amitābha, he realized it was exactly as he had seen it on the way. He marveled at the wondrous conditions of such a response and recognized the intensity of the Buddha’s compassion.

Upon arrival, he immediately entered the hall to listen to the lectures along with the assembly. The late Master Xie’an, Elder Brother Ding Zhuoya, was commissioned to lecture on the *Wusheng lun* (Treatise on Non-arising).
Through this, [the author] attained entry into the ultimate principles of the teachings and doctrines; consequently, he resolved to carve woodblocks for a commentary on this treatise.
To bestow grace upon future students, I lamented that there might be instances of verbosity or error in this commemorative text.
I therefore requested my elder brother, Shao-tan Cheng, to re-examine and revise it before entrusting it to the carver. Thus have I recorded its origins.
